parts.title: Booking a holiday cottage
parts.intro: You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman and an agent at a holiday cottage company.

script.t: Good morning, Brookfield Cottages, Daniel speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hello. I’m hoping to book one of your cottages for a family holiday this summer.
Certainly. Have you stayed with us before?
No, it’s the first time. A friend recommended you.
Lovely. Then I’ll just need to take a few details. Could I have your surname, please?
Yes, it’s Hollins. H, O, double L, I, N, S.
script.say: Yes, it’s Hollins. H, O, double L, I, N, S.

script.t: Thank you. And your first name?
Margaret, but everyone calls me Maggie.
I’ll put Margaret on the booking. And what’s the best number to contact you on?
My mobile is probably best. It’s 07734 218965.
script.say: My mobile is probably best. It’s oh seven seven three four, two one eight, nine six five.

script.t: Let me read that back: 07734 218965.
script.say: Let me read that back: oh seven seven three four, two one eight, nine six five.

script.t: That’s right.
Now, which dates were you thinking of?
We’d like to arrive on the 12th of August. No, sorry, I’m looking at the wrong calendar. It’s the 14th, a Saturday.
script.say: We’d like to arrive on the twelfth of August. No, sorry, I’m looking at the wrong calendar. It’s the fourteenth, a Saturday.

script.t: The 14th of August, and for how many nights?
script.say: The fourteenth of August, and for how many nights?

script.t: A week, so seven nights.
Fine. And how many people will there be in your party?
Two adults and three children. The youngest is only two, so we’ll need a cot if possible.
That’s no problem at all; all our larger cottages have a cot available. Do you have a particular cottage in mind?
My friend stayed in one called Willow Cottage and loved it.
Ah, Willow is already booked that week, I’m afraid. But Harbour Cottage is free, and it’s actually a bit bigger. It sleeps six.
Oh, that sounds fine. Is it near the sea?
It’s about five minutes’ walk from the beach, and there’s a garden at the back where the children can play.
Perfect. We’ll take it.
Now, let me tell you about the price. For that week in August, Harbour Cottage costs £780.
script.say: Now, let me tell you about the price. For that week in August, Harbour Cottage costs seven hundred and eighty pounds.

script.t: Does that include everything?
It includes electricity and heating, and towels and bed linen. The only extra is if you bring a dog.
No, no pets, thank goodness. What about a deposit?
We ask for a deposit of 25% when you book, and the rest is due six weeks before you arrive.
script.say: We ask for a deposit of twenty-five percent when you book, and the rest is due six weeks before you arrive.

script.t: OK. And how do we get the keys? We probably won’t arrive until quite late.
Some companies use an office in the village, but we don’t. The keys will be in a small safe beside the front door. We’ll text you the code the day before.
That’s very convenient. Is there anywhere to park?
Yes, there’s space for two cars in front of the cottage, so you won’t need to use the public car park.
Great. One more thing. Is there internet? My husband may need to do a little work.
There is wi-fi, although I should warn you that it can be slow in the evenings when everyone in the village is online.
Hmm, he’ll survive. Are there any shops nearby?
There’s a small supermarket in the village, but most guests prefer the farmers’ market on Wednesday mornings. The local cheese is famous.
Wonderful. And can we leave the cottage late on our last day?
Normally guests leave by ten in the morning, but if nobody is arriving that day we can let you stay until midday. We’ll confirm that nearer the time.
That would be helpful. Thank you so much, Daniel.
My pleasure. I’ll email the booking form to you this afternoon.

parts.title: Welcome to Ashdown Botanical Garden
parts.intro: You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a botanical garden.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Ashdown Botanical Garden. My name’s Clare and I’ll be your guide for the first part of your visit.

Before we set off, let me tell you a little about the garden. It was opened more than a hundred years ago by a local doctor who wanted to grow plants for medicine. These days, of course, we’re much more interested in protecting rare species.

Many visitors assume the garden is run by the town council, but in fact it belongs to a charity, and most of the work is done by volunteers. We have around sixty of them, and without them we simply couldn’t open.
A few practical points. You’re welcome to take photographs anywhere in the garden, but please don’t use a tripod in the glasshouses, as the paths there are quite narrow.
Picnics are allowed on the main lawn only. And although the garden is very quiet on weekday mornings, it gets extremely busy at weekends, so if you come back, try to come early.

Now, our most popular event is the night walk in the winter, when the trees are lit up. The summer concerts used to be our biggest event, but these days it’s definitely the night walk that sells out first.
Right, if you look at the map I gave you, you’ll see we’re standing at the main gate at the bottom of the map, on Mill Lane.
The main path goes straight ahead, north, from here. The first building on your left as you walk up the path is the shop, where you can buy seeds and books.
Opposite the shop, on the right of the path, is the café. It’s small but the cakes are excellent.

Keep going along the main path and you’ll reach the fountain in the centre of the garden. From the fountain, if you take the path to the right, it leads you to the big glasshouse, which is in the north-east corner of the garden.
The rose garden is in the opposite corner, the north-west, but at the moment it’s closed while we replant it.

If you want somewhere quieter, there’s the pond. To find it, walk up the main path from the gate and, just after you pass the café, turn right onto a narrow path. The pond is at the end of that path, in the south-east corner.

And finally, the children’s play area. It’s on the left side of the garden, between the shop and the rose garden, so you’ll see it on your left as you walk from the shop towards the fountain. It’s right next to the woods.
OK, any questions before we start? No? Then follow me.

parts.title: Planning a presentation on campus plastic waste
parts.intro: You will hear two students, Omar and Lucy, talking to their tutor about a presentation on reducing plastic waste at their university.

script.t: Come in, both of you. So, how’s the presentation coming along?
Quite well, I think. We decided to focus on single-use plastic in the university cafés rather than across the whole campus.
That’s sensible. Why did you narrow it down?
At first we wanted to look at everything, including the labs, but we realised we couldn’t get reliable figures for the labs. The cafés keep very detailed records of what they buy.
Good. And how did you collect your own data?
We thought about interviewing café staff, but they were too busy. So in the end we counted the items left in the bins at three cafés over a week.
That must have been unpleasant.
It wasn’t too bad. The surprising thing was what we found. We expected coffee cups to be the biggest problem, but it was actually the plastic lids and stirrers. There were far more of those.
Interesting. Have you thought about how you’ll present that?
We were going to use a pie chart, but there are too many categories, so we’ve gone for a simple bar chart instead.
Fine. Now, the main thing I wanted to talk about is your recommendations.
You’ve listed several possible solutions. Let’s go through them. What about charging extra for disposable cups?
Personally I think that’s the most effective option. Students are very sensitive to price.
I agree it would work, but I’m worried it would be unpopular, and the student union would probably oppose it. So we’ve recommended it, but as a long-term step.
And giving away free reusable bottles?
We looked into it, but other universities found that most students lose them within weeks, so we decided not to include it.
What about water fountains?
There are only four on the whole campus, and two of them are broken. Repairing them would cost very little, so we think it should happen immediately.
I agree. And the idea of an app?
Oh, the app where students get points for using their own cup. Lucy wasn’t keen.
It’s not that I dislike it, but it would need a lot of money to develop, and we don’t know who would pay for it. So we’ve said it needs further research.
Fair enough. Finally, the labels on the bins?
Yes, at the moment people put plastic in the wrong bin all the time because the signs are confusing. Clearer labels are cheap and easy, so that’s another one for straight away.
Good work. Make sure your timing is right: you’ve only got fifteen minutes.

parts.title: The history of salt
parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of salt production and trade.

script.t: Good afternoon. Today we’re going to look at a substance that most of us take completely for granted: salt. It may seem ordinary, but for thousands of years it was one of the most valuable goods in the world.

So why was salt so important? The main reason is that, before refrigeration, it was the only reliable way to preserve food. Meat and fish packed in salt could be kept for months, which allowed people to survive the winter and to travel long distances.
Salt was also essential for animals. Farmers needed it to keep their cattle healthy, and in some regions salt was even used as a form of money.

There have traditionally been three main ways of producing salt. The simplest is to let seawater evaporate in shallow pools, using the heat of the sun. This method works best in places with a hot, dry climate and little rain.

In colder, wetter places, people boiled seawater or the water from salt springs in large metal pans over a fire. This required huge amounts of fuel, usually wood, and in some areas whole forests were cut down.
The third method is mining. Underground deposits of rock salt were left behind when ancient seas dried up millions of years ago. Mining was dangerous and the work was extremely hard.

Now let’s turn to trade. Because salt was heavy and needed in such large quantities, transporting it shaped the routes people used. Many ancient routes in Europe were originally created for carrying salt.

Across the Sahara, camel caravans carried slabs of salt south for weeks. In the markets at the end of the journey, salt was exchanged for gold, sometimes at equal weight, which shows just how much it was valued.
Of course, a product this valuable attracted governments. Rulers quickly realised that salt could be taxed, and because everyone needed it, the tax was almost impossible to avoid.

Unsurprisingly, salt taxes were deeply unpopular, especially among the poor, for whom salt made up a large part of their spending. In several countries, anger about the salt tax contributed to protests and even revolts.

So what changed? In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, new technology made salt cheap. Refrigeration and canning reduced the need for salt as a preservative, and industrial production made it abundant.
Today, interestingly, most salt produced in the world is not eaten at all. It is used by industry, particularly in making chemicals.
And a large amount is spread on roads in winter to stop them freezing, which is why you may see piles of it beside motorways.

And that brings us to a final point about health. While salt was once scarce, many people now eat far too much of it, mostly hidden in processed food. So a substance that once kept people alive is now something doctors warn us about.
